title: Queues: enqueue, dequeue, front/rear and circular queues
learningObjectives: Explain FIFO ordering and distinguish enqueue, dequeue, peek and rear operations.
Represent a bounded circular queue with an array, front index and element count.
Calculate the rear insertion index with modular arithmetic and explain wrap-around.
Implement enqueue, dequeue and peek with explicit success or failure results.
Handle empty, full, wrap-around and nonzero-capacity constraints safely.
Compare circular queues with shifting queues and identify practical queue applications.

understand.concept: A queue is an abstract data type that normally follows first-in, first-out (FIFO): the first value inserted is the first value removed. Enqueue adds at the rear; dequeue removes from the front; peek reads the front without removing it. A circular array queue treats the array as a ring, wrapping an index to zero when it reaches the end.
understand.whyItMatters: Queues model waiting lines, print jobs, network buffers and breadth-first search. A circular queue reuses slots released by dequeue instead of shifting every remaining element.
understand.analogy: Imagine a boarding line: a new passenger joins at the back and the next passenger boards from the front. A circular buffer reuses a fixed set of positions after earlier items leave.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not explain index arithmetic, fixed capacity, memory representation or failure reporting. A program must distinguish a full queue from an empty one.

explain.narrative:
Use three pieces of state: data[capacity], front and count. Maintain the invariant 0 <= count <= capacity and 0 <= front < capacity. The next rear insertion position is (front + count) % capacity. Enqueue checks count < capacity before writing, stores the value at that position, then increments count. Dequeue checks count > 0 before reading, copies data[front] to the caller, advances front with (front + 1) % capacity, then decrements count. Peek reads data[front] without changing state.

A count field distinguishes empty and full states even when circular indices coincide. Modulo is safe only when capacity is nonzero. In this example capacity is a compile-time constant. If capacity is supplied at runtime, reject zero before any modulo operation and ensure the backing array really has that many elements.

A failed enqueue or dequeue must not partially modify the queue. Return bool to report success and use an output pointer for a dequeued value; do not reserve an ordinary integer such as -1 as an error marker because it may be valid data. Queue operations take O(1) time and the fixed array uses O(capacity) storage.

examples.title: Circular queue with safe enqueue, dequeue and peek
examples.explanation: The queue stores 10, 20 and 30. Removing 10 advances front. Adding 40 and 50 reuses freed positions, demonstrating wrap-around. Another enqueue fails because the queue is full. The remaining dequeue order is 20, 30, 40, 50, confirming FIFO behaviour.

examples.title: Calculate the next rear index
examples.explanation: (3 + 4) % 5 equals 2, so the next insertion uses index 2. Modulo wraps the position into the valid array range. This calculation assumes capacity is nonzero and the queue invariant is valid.

practise.guidedTask: For a queue of capacity 4, perform enqueue(7), enqueue(8), enqueue(9), dequeue(), enqueue(10), enqueue(11), peek() and dequeue(). After each operation record front, count, logical queue contents and next rear index. Then attempt one more enqueue and explain why it fails.
practise.independentTask: Implement a circular queue of characters with enqueue, dequeue, peek and is_empty. Test empty, exactly full, one extra enqueue, repeated wrap-around, FIFO order and null output pointers. Verify that failed operations leave the queue unchanged.
hints: The logical rear insertion index is (front + count) % capacity.
Check full before writing and empty before reading.
Advance front with (front + 1) % capacity after a successful dequeue.
Update count only after the operation has safely completed.
A count field distinguishes full and empty states even when indices coincide.
Never use modulo with zero capacity; validate runtime capacity first.

questions.prompt: Which ordering rule does a normal queue follow?
questions.explanation: FIFO means the earliest inserted item is the first item removed.

questions.prompt: Which expression gives the next rear insertion index?
questions.explanation: Adding count to front locates the next logical free position; modulo capacity wraps it into the array range.

questions.prompt: What should enqueue do when count equals capacity?
options: Return failure without changing the queue
questions.answer: Return failure without changing the queue
questions.explanation: A bounded queue is full at count == capacity and must not overwrite or write beyond its logical capacity.

questions.prompt: What should dequeue do when the queue is empty?
questions.explanation: Checking count before reading prevents access to an item that is not present.

questions.prompt: Why is a circular queue more efficient than shifting after each dequeue?
options: It advances indices and reuses freed slots in O(1) time
It allocates a new array each time
It removes full and empty checks
questions.answer: It advances indices and reuses freed slots in O(1) time
questions.explanation: Circular indexing avoids moving the remaining elements while preserving FIFO order.
